text:
Rivers are the arteries of the land. They begin modestly, as trickles of snowmelt or springwater on high ground, and gather strength as tributaries join them on their long descent toward the sea. Along the way they carve valleys, deposit fertile silt, and shape the landscapes through which they pass. The Grand Canyon is the patient work of the Colorado. The Nile delta is a gift of mud carried from the Ethiopian highlands.

Human history has followed rivers closely. The earliest cities rose along the Tigris, Euphrates, Indus, and Yellow River, where reliable water meant reliable harvests. Rivers served as highways before roads existed, carrying goods, people, and ideas between settlements. Many of the world's great capitals still sit on their banks: London on the Thames, Paris on the Seine, Cairo on the Nile.

Rivers are also living systems. They host fish, birds, insects, and plants that depend on seasonal floods and clean flow. Dams, pollution, and overuse have damaged many of them, yet restoration efforts show that rivers can recover when given the chance.

A river is never the same twice. It is always arriving and always leaving, a reminder that change itself can be constant and life-giving.
